subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 14! In this unit you will become a pattern detective and a chance explorer. Patterns are all around you, every single day. When Amina lays out the rugs in neat rows, when Yusuf sees the stripes on his football shirt, or when Halima threads red and white beads for a bracelet, they are all working with patterns. And chance is everywhere too – when you toss a coin to decide who kicks first, or wonder whether it will rain before you walk to school, you are thinking about probability.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 2 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Recognise a repeating pattern and tell it apart from a random muddle.
Find the rule (the part that repeats) in a pattern and name it, such as AB or ABC.
Copy, continue and create repeating patterns with colours, shapes, sounds and movements.
Fill in the missing part of a pattern by using its rule.
Tell the difference between a repeating pattern and a growing pattern.
Use the chance words certain, likely, unlikely and impossible correctly.
Say whether one event is more likely, less likely or equally likely than another.

concepts.title: What Makes Something a Pattern?
concepts.explanation:
A pattern is not just any group of things. A pattern is things arranged so that a part repeats in a set order, over and over, in a way you can predict. That word predict is the heart of it: if you can look at what has come so far and know what comes next, you are looking at a pattern.

Imagine Aisha threads beads on a string for a bracelet like this: red, white, red, white, red, white. You can feel the beat of it, can you not? Red, white… red, white… If someone hid the string and asked, ‘What bead comes next?’ you would answer ‘red’ with confidence, because the beads follow a rule. Now imagine a different string: red, red, white, blue, white, red, blue. This time you cannot be sure what comes next, because there is no rule repeating. The first string is a pattern; the second is a random arrangement.

Patterns do not have to be made of colours. They can be shapes (circle, triangle, circle, triangle), sounds (clap, stamp, clap, stamp), movements (jump, spin, jump, spin), or even the days that repeat each week. What every pattern shares is a part that comes again and again in the same order. When Hassan claps clap-clap-pause, clap-clap-pause across the room, everyone can join in after one or two rounds, because their ears have caught the rule.
concepts.example: So, three signs tell you that you are looking at a true pattern. First, something repeats. Second, it repeats in the same order every time. Third, you can use that to predict what comes next. If any of these is missing, you have a random muddle, not a pattern. Being able to tell these two apart is the very first skill of a pattern detective, and you will use it all the way through this unit.

concepts.title: Finding the Rule and Naming It
concepts.explanation:
Every repeating pattern has a rule – the little piece that repeats. Finding this piece is like finding the key to a door. Once you have it, the whole pattern opens up. To find the rule, look from the start and ask, ‘Where does the pattern begin to say the same thing again?’ That first chunk, up to the point where it repeats, is your rule.

Look at this pattern: mango, mango, banana, mango, mango, banana. Where does it start again? After ‘mango, mango, banana’ it says ‘mango, mango, banana’ once more. So the rule is mango, mango, banana. That repeating chunk is sometimes called the unit of the pattern.

To make patterns easy to talk about, mathematicians give the parts letters. The first kind of thing is A, the next new thing is B, the next new thing is C, and so on. This lets us name a pattern quickly without caring what it is made of:

AB pattern: red, blue, red, blue → A is red, B is blue. Sound version: clap, stamp, clap, stamp.

ABC pattern: red, blue, green, red, blue, green → three things repeat. Shape version: circle, square, triangle, circle, square, triangle.

AAB pattern: red, red, blue, red, red, blue → A comes twice, then B once.

ABB pattern: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue → A once, then B twice.

ABBC pattern: circle, square, square, triangle, circle, square, square, triangle → a longer four-part rule.

The clever thing about letters is that two patterns that look totally different can share the same rule. Red-blue-red-blue and clap-stamp-clap-stamp are both AB patterns, even though one is beads and the other is sound. And mango-mango-banana is an AAB pattern, just like Sahra jumping jump-jump-spin, jump-jump-spin. When you can hear the letters behind the things, you are thinking like a real mathematician.
concepts.example: Here is how Farah finds the rule step by step. She reads the pattern slowly from the left. She marks where it first starts to repeat. She reads that chunk out loud as letters. Then she checks her rule by reading the whole pattern in the beat of that rule to make sure it fits all the way along. If it fits, she has the rule; if it slips, she looks again. Checking your rule against the whole pattern is a habit that saves you from silly slips.

concepts.title: Copying, Continuing and Creating Patterns
concepts.explanation:
There are three things a pattern detective can do with a pattern, and they get a little harder each time. You can copy a pattern, you can continue a pattern, and you can create a brand-new pattern of your own. Let us take them one at a time.

Copying is the gentlest. Someone shows you red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue and you lay out the very same beads underneath: red, blue, blue, red, blue, blue. To copy well, look at one item at a time and match it. Copying trains your eyes to notice each part in order, which you need before you can do anything harder.

Continuing means carrying a pattern onward. You are given the start – say, green, yellow, green, yellow, green, ___ – and you must add what comes next. To do this, first find the rule (here it is AB: green, yellow), then keep the beat going. After green comes yellow. If they asked for three more, you would add yellow, green, yellow. Always find the rule first; never just guess from the last item alone.
concepts.example: Creating is the most fun. Here you invent your own rule and then build the pattern to match it. Maybe Ibrahim decides on an ABC rule using stones, leaves and shells: stone, leaf, shell, stone, leaf, shell, stone, leaf, shell. A good pattern maker decides on the rule first, then lays out the pieces carefully, and finally checks the whole line to make sure the rule holds from start to finish. When you create a pattern for a friend to continue, you are giving them a lovely puzzle to solve.

concepts.title: Missing Parts and Repeating vs Growing Patterns
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes a pattern has a gap in the middle, and your job is to fill it. This is trickier than continuing, because you cannot just look at the end – you must use the rule to work out what belongs in the hole. Take this one: red, blue, ___, red, blue, green, red, blue, green. The rule is ABC (red, blue, green), so the gap must be green. The way to solve a gap is always the same: find the rule from the parts you can see, then place the missing term the rule demands.

There is also a second family of patterns you should meet: growing patterns. A repeating pattern says the same thing over and over, but a growing pattern gets bigger (or smaller) each step. Think of towers of blocks: 1 block, then 2 blocks, then 3 blocks, then 4 blocks. Nothing repeats here – instead, one more block is added each time. Another growing pattern is 2, 4, 6, 8, where you add two each step. Growing patterns still have a rule, but the rule is about how much it changes, not about a chunk that repeats.

How do you tell the two apart? Ask yourself: ‘Does a chunk come again and again in the same order?’ If yes, it is a repeating pattern. Or ask: ‘Does each step get bigger or smaller by the same amount?’ If yes, it is a growing pattern. Zahra keeps it simple: repeating patterns dance in a circle, coming back to where they began, while growing patterns climb a staircase, always reaching higher. Both are patterns, because both let you predict what comes next – they just follow different kinds of rules.
concepts.example: Most of your work in Stage 2 is with repeating patterns, so if you are ever unsure, look first for a chunk that repeats. But it is good to know that growing patterns exist, because you will meet many more of them in later units when you count in twos, fives and tens, which are really growing patterns in disguise.

concepts.title: The Language of Chance
concepts.explanation:
Now we turn from patterns to probability, which is a big word for a simple idea: how likely something is to happen. Some things are sure, some things can never happen, and many things are somewhere in between. Mathematicians use four special words to describe where an event sits, and you will use them all through this unit.

Certain means it will definitely happen – there is no doubt at all. It is certain that the sun will rise tomorrow. It is certain that if a bag holds only red beans, the bean you draw will be red. Impossible is the opposite: it can never happen, no matter what. It is impossible to draw a blue bean from a bag of only red beans. It is impossible to roll a 7 on an ordinary die that only shows 1 to 6.

Between these two live most everyday events. Likely means it will probably happen, though it is not completely sure. In Mogadishu it is likely to be hot at midday. Unlikely means it will probably not happen, though it just might. It is unlikely that Omar will pull the single red bean out of a bag full of white beans on his very first try – it could happen, but probably it will not.
concepts.example: A lovely way to picture these four words is as a line, like a road with certainty at one end and impossibility at the other. Impossible sits at the far left. Certain sits at the far right. Unlikely is a little way in from the impossible end, and likely is a little way in from the certain end. Every event can be placed somewhere on this road of chance. When Maryam wonders whether her football team will win on Friday, she does not say ‘yes’ or ‘no’ – she says ‘likely’ or ‘unlikely’, and that is much wiser, because nobody can be certain about a game.

concepts.title: Comparing How Likely Events Are
concepts.explanation:
It is useful not only to describe one event, but to compare two events and say which is more likely. For this we use three phrases: more likely, less likely and equally likely. Comparing chances is often easier than it sounds, because you can look at the objects and count.

Think of a bag with 8 red beans and 2 white beans. If you close your eyes and draw one bean, are you more likely to get red or white? There are far more red beans, so drawing red is more likely and drawing white is less likely. The colour with more beans wins the better chance. Now think of a bag with 5 red beans and 5 white beans. Here red and white have the same number, so drawing red and drawing white are equally likely. Nobody has the edge.

The same idea works for a spinner – a circle split into coloured parts with an arrow that spins. If the spinner has a big green part and a small yellow part, the arrow is more likely to stop on green, because green covers more of the circle. If green and yellow take up equal halves, the two colours are equally likely. Larger part, better chance; smaller part, poorer chance. When Noor designs a spinner so that landing on ‘win’ is very unlikely, she makes the ‘win’ slice very thin.
concepts.example: A coin is the fairest chance of all. A coin has just two sides, heads and tails, and both are the same size, so heads and tails are equally likely. This is why we toss a coin to decide who starts a game – it gives nobody an unfair advantage. When Liban and Abdi cannot agree who kicks the ball first, a coin toss settles it fairly, because each boy has an equal chance.

methods.title: How to find and continue a pattern
methods.example: Work through these with me. Cover the solution, try it yourself first, then check every step.
steps: Read the pattern from the start and find where it repeats.
Name the repeating chunk as letters (AB, ABC, AAB…).
Check the rule fits all along the pattern.
Keep the rule going to add the next terms, or to fill a gap.

methods.title: How to judge how likely an event is
methods.example: Give the letter name for this pattern: circle, square, square, circle, square, square.
steps: Ask: can it never happen? Then it is impossible.
Ask: will it definitely happen? Then it is certain.
Check your answer by asking a friend if they agree it is impossible, certain, or in between.

methods.title: How to compare two events
methods.example: Carry this on for three more terms: green, yellow, green, yellow, green, ___, ___, ___.
steps: To compare two events, count the objects — more objects means more likely.
Compare the counts directly: whichever event has more matching objects is more likely to happen.
Check your answer by re-counting each group once more.

methods.title: How to run a chance experiment
methods.example: Find the missing term: red, blue, green, red, ___, green, red, blue, green.
steps: Predict what you think will happen.
Do the test many times in the same fair way.
Record each result with a tally mark.
Count and compare your results with your prediction.

methods.title: Certain, likely, unlikely or impossible?
methods.example: Find the missing term: red, blue, green, red, ___, green, red, blue, green.
steps: The rule is ABC (red, blue, green).
After red should come blue, so the gap is blue.
Check it: red, blue, green, red, blue, green, red, blue, green — the rule holds all the way, so blue is correct.

workedExamples.title: Is it a pattern?
workedExamples.prompt: Look at this: red, white, red, white, red, white. Is it a pattern? What about: red, white, blue, red, green, white?
workedExamples.solution: The first one is a pattern, because the chunk 'red, white' repeats in the same order over and over, so you can predict red comes next. The second one is not a pattern — no chunk repeats in order, so you cannot predict what comes next. It is a random arrangement.

workedExamples.title: Name the rule
workedExamples.prompt: Give the letter name for this pattern: circle, square, square, circle, square, square.
workedExamples.solution: The repeating chunk is ‘circle, square, square’. Circle is the first new thing (A) and square is the second new thing (B), and square repeats, so the pattern is ABB. It fits all the way along: A-B-B, A-B-B.

workedExamples.title: Continue the pattern
workedExamples.prompt: Carry this on for three more terms: green, yellow, green, yellow, green, ___, ___, ___.
workedExamples.solution: The rule is AB (green, yellow). The last shown term is green, so next comes yellow, then green, then yellow. The full carry-on is yellow, green, yellow.

workedExamples.title: Fill the missing part
workedExamples.prompt: Find the missing term: red, blue, green, red, ___, green, red, blue, green.
workedExamples.solution: The rule is ABC (red, blue, green). After red should come blue, so the gap is blue. Check it: red, blue, green, red, blue, green, red, blue, green — the rule holds all the way, so blue is correct.

workedExamples.title: Certain, likely, unlikely or impossible?
workedExamples.prompt: A bag holds only white beans. Choose the right word for each: (a) drawing a white bean, (b) drawing a red bean.
workedExamples.solution: (a) Drawing a white bean is certain, because every bean in the bag is white. (b) Drawing a red bean is impossible, because there are no red beans in the bag to draw.

workedExamples.title: More likely or less likely?
workedExamples.prompt: A spinner has a big green section and a small yellow section. When you spin it, are you more likely to land on green or on yellow?
workedExamples.solution: The green section covers much more of the spinner than the yellow section, so there is more space for the arrow to land on green. Landing on green is more likely, and landing on yellow is less likely.

workedExamples.title: The fair coin
workedExamples.prompt: Amina tosses a fair coin. It lands on heads three times in a row. On the next toss, is heads or tails more likely?
workedExamples.solution: Neither! Heads and tails are still equally likely, because a coin has no memory. Each toss starts fresh with two equal sides, so what happened before does not change the next toss.

workedExamples.title: Order by likelihood
workedExamples.prompt: Put these three events in order from most likely to least likely: (a) it will be hot tomorrow in Kismaayo, (b) you will roll a 3 on a die, (c) a goat will fly over the house.
workedExamples.solution: (a) Hot weather in Kismaayo is likely. (b) Rolling a 3 is possible but not very likely (one chance out of six). (c) A flying goat is impossible. So from most to least likely: (a), (b), (c).

workedExamples.title: Continue for three more terms: A, B, B, A, B, B, ___…
workedExamples.prompt: Continue for three more terms: A, B, B, A, B, B, ___, ___, ___.

workedExamples.title: Sort these into certain / likely / unlikely /…
workedExamples.prompt: Sort these into certain / likely / unlikely / impossible: a) it will rain in the wet season, b) rolling a 6 on a die, c) a goat will fly, d) night will come after day.
workedExamples.solution: a) likely, b) unlikely (one chance in six), c) impossible, d) certain.

workedExamples.title: True or False: after a coin lands heads three times…
workedExamples.prompt: True or False: after a coin lands heads three times, tails is more likely next. Explain.
workedExamples.solution: False — a coin has no memory, so heads and tails stay equally likely.

workedExamples.title: Create an ABBC pattern using four different things…
workedExamples.prompt: Create an ABBC pattern using four different things from your home and write it for eight terms.
workedExamples.solution: Any correct ABBC pattern, e.g. stone, leaf, leaf, shell, stone, leaf, leaf, shell.

activities.title: Bead or Button Pattern String
activities.materials: beads, buttons, or dry beans in two or three colours, and a string or piece of thread.
steps: Choose a rule, such as AB (red, white) or ABC (red, white, blue).
Thread the beads to follow your rule for at least three repeats.
Say your pattern out loud as you go: ‘red, white, red, white…’
Ask a family member to continue your string with the next three beads.
Keep your string – you can make a new rule each day of the unit.

activities.title: Sound and Movement Patterns
activities.materials: just your hands, feet and voice.
steps: Make a sound pattern like clap, stamp, clap, stamp (an AB pattern).
Try a longer rule such as clap, clap, stamp (an AAB pattern).
Perform your pattern for someone and let them join in once they hear the rule.
Swap: they make a pattern and you find the rule and continue it.

activities.title: The Coin Toss Experiment
activities.materials: one coin, paper and a pencil.
steps: Make two columns on your paper: one for heads, one for tails.
Predict what will happen before you start – write your guess down.
Toss the coin ten times and put a tally mark in the right column each time.
Count each column. How close was your result to your guess? Try it again and compare.
This game shows you that a fair coin gives heads and tails an equal chance, even if ten tosses come out a little uneven.

activities.title: Mystery Bag Investigation
activities.materials: a cloth bag or bowl you cannot see into, and beans, stones or buttons in two colours.
steps: Put in a mix, such as 8 white beans and 2 red beans.
Predict: which colour are you more likely to draw?
Draw one, look, and put it back. Do this ten times, tallying the colours.
Did you draw more of the colour you expected? Talk about why with your family.

activities.title: The Chance Word Sorting Game (Family Game)
activities.materials: your family or friends, and four spots on the floor labelled certain, likely, unlikely and impossible.
steps: One person calls out an event, such as ‘it will get dark tonight’.
Everyone runs to stand on the chance word they think fits best.
Talk about any differences – some events sit between two words!
Take turns being the caller and try to think of tricky events.

activities.title: Design-a-Spinner Challenge
activities.materials: paper, a pencil, colouring pens, and a paper clip for the arrow.
steps: Draw a circle and split it into coloured parts.
Make one colour cover most of the circle and another cover only a thin slice.
Predict which colour the arrow is most likely to land on, and which is unlikely.
Spin many times using a pencil and paper clip, and tally where the arrow stops.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand patterns best? Which helped you understand chance best? What was the trickiest part? What would you like more practice with? Share your answer with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Pattern Rule
rules.text: A pattern has a chunk that repeats in the same order over and over. The repeating chunk is called the rule, for example AB or ABC. If nothing repeats, it is a random muddle, not a pattern.

rules.title: Chance Words Rule
rules.text: Certain = it will definitely happen. Impossible = it can never happen. Likely = it will probably happen. Unlikely = it will probably not happen. Compare chances with: more likely, less likely, equally likely.

rules.title: Fair Coin Rule
rules.text: A coin has two equal sides, so heads and tails are equally likely. A coin has no memory – past tosses do not change the next toss.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in The Language of Chance.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Now we turn from patterns to probability, which is a big word for a simple idea: how likely something is to happen. Some things are sure, some things can never happen, and many things are somewhere in between. Mathematicians use four special words to describe where an event sits, and you will use them all through this unit.

Certain means it will definitely happen – there is no doubt at all. It is certain that the sun will rise tomorrow. It is certain that if a bag holds only red beans, the bean you draw will be red. Impossible is the opposite: it can never happen, no matter what. It is impossible to draw a blue bean from a bag of only red beans. It is impossible to roll a 7 on an ordinary die that only shows 1 to 6.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Comparing How Likely Events Are.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
It is useful not only to describe one event, but to compare two events and say which is more likely. For this we use three phrases: more likely, less likely and equally likely. Comparing chances is often easier than it sounds, because you can look at the objects and count.

Think of a bag with 8 red beans and 2 white beans. If you close your eyes and draw one bean, are you more likely to get red or white? There are far more red beans, so drawing red is more likely and drawing white is less likely. The colour with more beans wins the better chance. Now think of a bag with 5 red beans and 5 white beans. Here red and white have the same number, so drawing red and drawing white are equally likely. Nobody has the edge.

games.title: Unit Champion: Certain / Impossible
games.description: Four short challenges on Certain / Impossible.

rounds.prompt: What does “Repeating pattern” mean?
choices: The same unit comes again and again
Will definitely happen / can never happen
Will probably / probably will not happen
rounds.answer: The same unit comes again and again
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 14 Maths Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Repeating pattern means the same unit comes again and again.

rounds.prompt: Continue the pattern: sun, moon, sun, moon, sun, ___.
rounds.clue: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.
rounds.explanation: The rule is AB (sun, moon); after sun comes moon.

rounds.prompt: Which chance word describes an event that will definitely happen?
rounds.clue: Rule out the options you know are wrong, then check the one that is left.
rounds.explanation: Certain means it will definitely happen, with no doubt at all.

rounds.prompt: Which set of beads is arranged in a pattern rather than a muddle: (a) red, white, red, white, red, white or (b) red, white, blue, red, green, white?
choices: (a) is a pattern, (b) is a muddle
(b) is a pattern, (a) is a muddle
rounds.answer: (a) is a pattern, (b) is a muddle
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: In (a) the chunk 'red, white' repeats in order so you can predict what comes next; in (b) nothing repeats in order.

selfAssessment: I can recognise a repeating pattern and tell it apart from a random muddle.
I can find the rule (the part that repeats) in a pattern and name it, such as AB or ABC.
I can copy, continue and create repeating patterns with colours, shapes, sounds and movements.
I can fill in the missing part of a pattern by using its rule.
I can tell the difference between a repeating pattern and a growing pattern.
I can use the chance words certain, likely, unlikely and impossible correctly.
I can say whether one event is more likely, less likely or equally likely than another.
